newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen leader says Russia sabotaging elections.
newsitem.headline: Chechen leader says Russia sabotaging elections.

text.p: Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, president of the self-declared Chechen Republic, accused Moscow of trying to sabotage next week's elections, which he hopes will give him a popular mandate to lead the region to independence.

The bearded, soft-voiced poet told reporters in his Grozny office late on Saturday that Russian intelligence services were behind the murders of six foreign Red Cross workers in December as well as other recent crimes against civilians in Chechnya.

"We have a circle of suspects who...worked with the Russian intelligence services," Yandarbiyev said of the brutal killings, which forced the withdrawal of all foreign aid workers. Russian officials have consistently denied accusations of complicity.

Yandarbiyev, nominated Chechen leader after the death in a rocket attack last April of the charismatic Dzhokhar Dudayev, faces 15 other candidates and, especially, four other senior figures in the rebel guerrilla army that forced President Boris Yeltsin to withdraw his troops after nearly two years of war.
All the leading candidates in the January 27 presidential vote, which is accompanied by voting for a regional assembly, have pledged to press for full secession from Russia.
Yandarbiyev said Russia had resorted to covert "provocations" to destabilise Chechnya ahead of the vote.
"This is a malicious policy organised at the top levels of the Russian government. They don't want peace or stability."
Yandarbiyev said the recent kidnapping of two Russian Orthodox priests and pledges by top Russian officials to protect ethnic Russians in the region were aimed at smearing Chechnya.
"All the roads and crimes lead to Moscow," he said.

Russian news agencies said on Sunday that Yandarbiyev and other Chechen leaders ordered a stepping up of security measures at a meeting on Saturday. Yandarbiyev campaign aides said on Sunday his office was slightly damaged by vandals overnight.

The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) will send several dozen observers to monitor voting but says it cannot guarantee their safety. Some observers have said they will stay away because of security fears.
Russia's best-known human rights activist, Sergei Kovalyov, accused the Chechens of "naivety" in refusing to set up voting stations for war refugees living in Moscow and other cities.

Kovalyov, a former Soviet dissident who spent weeks in Grozny bunkers braving Russian air raids two years ago, told Chechen vice-president Said-Khasan Abumuslimov on Saturday that refusing to include the refugees was a "serious mistake" which would be used in Moscow to question the legitimacy of the vote.
Russian officials say the lack of voting outside the region will disadvantage ethnic Russian refugees who oppose secession.
Kovalyov's successor as Yeltsin's human rights adviser last week condemned the elections, to which Moscow agreed as part of a peace deal last autumn, as "blatantly undemocratic".
Some Russian sources say as much as a quarter of Chechnya's pre-war population of one million remain outside the region.
But Abumuslimov and other Chechen leaders contend that most refugees have already returned home. They fear refugee voting could be manipulated by Russian intelligence services.
"We have learned by bitter experience never to trust Moscow," said Abumuslimov. Refugees living in nearby areas will be able to vote at stations set up in Chechnya near the border.
Guerrilla field commander Salman Raduyev addressed a rally in central Grozny on Sunday to celebrate the anniversary of his escape from the village of Pervomaiskoye last January.
He, his men and dozens of civilian hostages broke through a ring of Russian armour after a siege of more than a week.
